The classical capacity of generalized amplitude-damping channels and its strong-converse exponent

Kun Fang ††thanks: kunfang@cuhk.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen,
Guangdong, 518172, China
October 6, 2026
Abstract

The classical capacity of a quantum channel generally requires regularization because input codewords may be entangled across channel uses. We remove this regularization for generalized amplitude-damping channels (GADCs) and determine their exact strong-converse exponent throughout the full parameter range. The exponent is a single-letter transform of the sandwiched Rényi Holevo information and is attained by product input codewords with collective decoding. The key ingredient is a decomposition of the joint output into positive operators whose triangular factors have identical scalar Gram matrices after norm compression. A sharp triangular Schatten-norm compression inequality then establishes maximum output norm multiplicativity for diagonally sandwiched GADCs tensored with arbitrary completely positive maps. This yields additivity of the sandwiched Rényi Holevo information at every order above one. Consequently, the classical capacity equals the known one-copy Holevo information and admits a scalar optimization. Thus, entangled input codewords improve neither the capacity nor the optimal exponential decay of decoding success above capacity.

1 Introduction

The classical capacity of a quantum channel is the highest rate at which classical information can be transmitted with vanishing error. The Holevo–Schumacher–Westmoreland theorem expresses this capacity as [Hol73, Hol98, SW97]

C⁡(𝒩)=limn→∞1n​χ​(𝒩⊗n),\displaystyle C({\cal N})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\chi({\cal N}^{\otimes n}), (1)

where χ\chi denotes the Holevo information. The optimization allows input states entangled across arbitrarily many channel uses, and this regularization is necessary in general [Has09]. A central question is therefore whether a channel’s one-copy Holevo information already determines its classical capacity. Even for qubit channels, removing the regularization requires control of outputs produced by arbitrary entangled inputs.

The generalized amplitude-damping channel (GADC) models a two-level system exchanging energy with a thermal environment [KSW20]. It describes spin relaxation in quantum devices, including superconducting circuits [CB08], and has applications to optical losses with low-temperature background noise [ZLW+17]. We write 𝒜γ,N{\cal A}_{\gamma,N} for the channel with damping probability γ\gamma and equilibrium occupation NN; its action is given in (8). The zero-temperature case N=0N=0 is the amplitude-damping channel.

The one-copy Holevo information of the GADC is known through a scalar optimization [HF07, KSW20]. Earlier work developed computable bounds on the regularized capacity [WXD18, KSW20, FF21, FST22]. Recently, Tang, Zhu, Bai, and Wang [TZBW26] determined the classical capacity of amplitude damping through a triangular block-matrix entropy inequality. Their result establishes Holevo additivity with arbitrary other channels for qubit channels admitting a pure output. A GADC with 0<γ,N<10<\gamma,N<1 has no pure output, so this criterion does not cover the finite-temperature case.

In this work, we resolve the regularization problem for the full GADC family and determine its exact strong-converse exponent. For a channel 𝒩\mathcal{N}, let Ps⋆​(n,r,𝒩)P_{\mathrm{s}}^{\star}(n,r;\mathcal{N}) denote the optimal average decoding success probability over nn uses with at least 2n​r2^{nr} messages. We allow arbitrary entangled input codewords and collective decoding, but no entanglement assistance. The strong-converse exponent is

Esc​(r,𝒩)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{sc}}(r,\mathcal{N}) =limn→∞−1nlogPs⋆(n,r;𝒩).\displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}-\frac{1}{n}\log P_{\mathrm{s}}^{\star}(n,r;\mathcal{N}). (2)

It describes the optimal exponential decay of decoding success at rates above the classical capacity. Cheng and Tomamichel [CT26, Theorem 5] proved that the limit exists for every r⩾0r\geqslant 0 and

Esc​(r,𝒩)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{sc}}(r,\mathcal{N}) =supα>1α−1α​[r−limn→∞1n​χ~α​(𝒩⊗n)].\displaystyle=\sup_{\alpha>1}\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\left[r-\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{N}^{\otimes n})\right]. (3)

Thus, determining the exponent reduces to removing the regularization of the sandwiched Rényi Holevo information χ~α\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}, defined in Section 2. In contrast to the entropy argument of [TZBW26], this approach requires control at every order α>1\alpha>1, not only in the limit α→1+\alpha\to 1^{+}.

Theorem 1 (Strong converse exponent).

For every γ,N∈[0,1]\gamma,N\in[0,1], α>1\alpha>1, and positive integer nn,

χ~α​(𝒜γ,N⊗n)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n}) =n​χ~α​(𝒜γ,N).\displaystyle=n\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}). (4)

For every r⩾0r\geqslant 0, the limit in (2) exists and satisfies

Esc​(r,𝒜γ,N)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{sc}}(r,{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}) =supα>1α−1α​[r−χ~α​(𝒜γ,N)].\displaystyle=\sup_{\alpha>1}\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}[r-\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})]. (5)

Taking α→1+\alpha\to 1^{+} in (4) gives the following capacity formula.

Corollary 2 (Classical capacity).

For every γ,N∈[0,1]\gamma,N\in[0,1],

C⁡(𝒜γ,N)\displaystyle C({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}) =χ⁡(𝒜γ,N).\displaystyle=\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}). (6)

The main task is to establish (4). We follow the norm-based approach of Wilde, Winter, and Yang [WWY14], which relates the sandwiched Rényi information radius to maximum output norms of sandwiched maps. Our main technical result establishes the required multiplicativity for GADCs sandwiched by arbitrary nonnegative diagonal operators (Theorem 4). Phase covariance makes these diagonal operators sufficient for the reference-state optimization. The construction decomposes the joint output into a convex combination of two positive operators with triangular factors. Replacing each block of these factors by its Schatten norm produces scalar matrices with identical Gram matrices. A sharp triangular norm-compression inequality bounds each term by the same one-copy output norm. This matching property makes the argument applicable even when the channel has no pure output.

The norm-compression proof extends the log-determinant method of [TZBW26] from entropy to fractional trace powers. It establishes the previously missing range 2<p<42<p<4, complementing the known range p⩾4p\geqslant 4 [Kin03, Aud08].

2 Preliminaries

All Hilbert spaces are finite dimensional. A state is a positive semidefinite operator of trace one, and id\operatorname{id} denotes the identity map. All logarithms are to base two unless written as ln\ln. We write S⁡(ρ)=−Tr⁡ρ​log⁡ρS(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}\rho\log\rho for the von Neumann entropy and h2​(x)=−x​log⁡x−(1−x)​log⁡(1−x)h_{2}(x)=-x\log x-(1-x)\log(1-x) for the binary entropy, with 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0.

An (n,M)(n,M) code for 𝒩\mathcal{N} consists of states ρ1,…,ρM\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{M} on the input space of 𝒩⊗n\mathcal{N}^{\otimes n} and a decoding positive operator-valued measure {Dm}m=1M\{D_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} on its output space. The decoding operators satisfy Dm⩾0D_{m}\geqslant 0 and ∑mDm=I\sum_{m}D_{m}=I. The optimal average success probability at rate rr is

Ps⋆​(n,r,𝒩)\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{s}}^{\star}(n,r;\mathcal{N}) =sup(n,M)​ codesM⩾2n​r1M​∑m=1MTr⁡[𝒩⊗n​(ρm)​Dm].\displaystyle=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}(n,M)\text{ codes}\\ M\geqslant 2^{nr}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal{N}^{\otimes n}(\rho_{m})D_{m}]. (7)

Inputs may be entangled across the nn channel uses, and decoding may be collective.

The channel and its one-copy Holevo information.

For γ,N∈[0,1]\gamma,N\in[0,1], the GADC acts as

𝒜γ,N:ρ(q,z):=(1−qzz∗q)⟼(1−tγ,N​(q)1−γ​z1−γ​z∗tγ,N​(q)),\displaystyle{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}:\quad\rho(q,z):=\begin{pmatrix}1-q&z\\ z^{*}&q\end{pmatrix}\quad\longmapsto\quad\begin{pmatrix}1-t_{\gamma,N}(q)&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,z\\ \sqrt{1-\gamma}\,z^{*}&t_{\gamma,N}(q)\end{pmatrix}, (8)

where q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1], |z|2⩽q⁡(1−q)|z|^{2}\leqslant q(1-q), and tγ,N​(q)=γ​N+(1−γ)​qt_{\gamma,N}(q)=\gamma N+(1-\gamma)q. The quantities qq and tγ,N​(q)t_{\gamma,N}(q) are the input and output probabilities of |1⟩|1\rangle. The channel is phase covariant: for Uθ=|0⟩​⟨0|+ei​θ|1⟩​⟨1|U_{\theta}=|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+e^{i\theta}|1\rangle\!\langle 1|,

𝒜γ,N​(Uθ​ρ​Uθ†)\displaystyle{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(U_{\theta}\rho U_{\theta}^{\dagger}) =Uθ​𝒜γ,N​(ρ)​Uθ†.\displaystyle=U_{\theta}{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(\rho)U_{\theta}^{\dagger}. (9)

For later use, define

|ψq±⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{q}^{\pm}\rangle =1−q​|0⟩±q​|1⟩,\displaystyle=\sqrt{1-q}|0\rangle\pm\sqrt{q}|1\rangle, (10)
𝒜γ,N​(|ψq+⟩​⟨ψq+|)\displaystyle{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|) =(1−tγ,N​(q)(1−γ)​q​(1−q)(1−γ)​q​(1−q)tγ,N​(q)),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}1-t_{\gamma,N}(q)&\sqrt{(1-\gamma)q(1-q)}\\ \sqrt{(1-\gamma)q(1-q)}&t_{\gamma,N}(q)\end{pmatrix}, (11)
Dγ,N​(q)\displaystyle D_{\gamma,N}(q) :=det𝒜γ,N​(|ψq+⟩​⟨ψq+|)\displaystyle:=\det{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|)
=γ⁡[(1−γ)​(q−N)2+N⁡(1−N)].\displaystyle=\gamma\big[(1-\gamma)(q-N)^{2}+N(1-N)\big]. (12)

By phase covariance, every pure input with probability qq of |1⟩|1\rangle has an output unitarily equivalent to 𝒜γ,N​(|ψq+⟩​⟨ψq+|){\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|). Its entropy is f​(Dγ,N​(q))f(D_{\gamma,N}(q)), where

f⁡(d)\displaystyle f(d) =h2​(1+1−4​d2),0⩽d⩽14.\displaystyle=h_{2}\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4d}}{2}\right),\qquad 0\leqslant d\leqslant\frac{1}{4}. (13)

For a channel 𝒩\mathcal{N}, its Holevo information is

χ⁡(𝒩)\displaystyle\chi(\mathcal{N}) =sup{px,ρx}[S⁡(∑xpx​𝒩​(ρx))−∑xpx​S​(𝒩⁡(ρx))],\displaystyle=\sup_{\{p_{x},\rho_{x}\}}\left[S\!\left(\sum_{x}p_{x}\mathcal{N}(\rho_{x})\right)-\sum_{x}p_{x}S(\mathcal{N}(\rho_{x}))\right], (14)

χ⁡(𝒜γ,N)\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}) =max0⩽q⩽1⁡[h2​(tγ,N​(q))−f⁡(Dγ,N​(q))].\displaystyle=\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\left[h_{2}(t_{\gamma,N}(q))-f(D_{\gamma,N}(q))\right]. (15)

For this ensemble, both outputs have entropy f​(Dγ,N​(q))f(D_{\gamma,N}(q)), while their average is diagonal with eigenvalues 1−tγ,N​(q)1-t_{\gamma,N}(q) and tγ,N​(q)t_{\gamma,N}(q).

Rényi information and sandwiched norms.

For α>1\alpha>1, the sandwiched Rényi divergence and the corresponding information radius of a channel are

D~α(ρ∥σ)\displaystyle\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}(\rho\|\sigma) =1α−1​log⁡Tr⁡[(σ1−α2​α​ρ​σ1−α2​α)α],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\operatorname{Tr}\left[\left(\sigma^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2\alpha}}\rho\sigma^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2\alpha}}\right)^{\alpha}\right], (16)

When this inclusion holds, negative powers are taken on the support of σ\sigma [MLDS+13, WWY14]. It obeys data processing for every α>1\alpha>1 [FL13]. This radius equals the sandwiched Rényi Holevo information. The identity was established for 1<α⩽21<\alpha\leqslant 2 by Wilde, Winter, and Yang [WWY14, Lemma 14] and holds for all α>1\alpha>1 [MO17, Proposition IV.2]. For a finite ensemble ℰ={px,ρx}\mathcal{E}=\{p_{x},\rho_{x}\}, let ωX​Bℰ=∑xpx​|x⟩​⟨x|⊗𝒩⁡(ρx)\omega_{XB}^{\mathcal{E}}=\sum_{x}p_{x}|x\rangle\!\langle x|\otimes\mathcal{N}(\rho_{x}) and ωXℰ=∑xpx​|x⟩​⟨x|\omega_{X}^{\mathcal{E}}=\sum_{x}p_{x}|x\rangle\!\langle x|. The ensemble representation of the channel information is then

χ~α​(𝒩)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{N}) =supℰI~α​(ℰ,𝒩).\displaystyle=\sup_{\mathcal{E}}\widetilde{I}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{E};\mathcal{N}). (18)

νp​(Φ)\displaystyle\nu_{p}(\Phi) =maxρ⩾0,Tr⁡ρ=1⁡‖Φ⁡(ρ)‖p,1⩽p⩽∞.\displaystyle=\max_{\rho\geqslant 0,\,\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1}\|\Phi(\rho)\|_{p},\qquad 1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty. (19)

χ~α​(𝒩)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{N}) =infσ>0,Tr⁡σ=1αα−1​log⁡να​(𝒩σ(1−α)/(2​α)).\displaystyle=\inf_{\sigma>0,\,\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}\log\nu_{\alpha}(\mathcal{N}_{\sigma^{(1-\alpha)/(2\alpha)}}). (21)

3 Additivity of Holevo Rényi information

We prove the additivity statement in Theorem 1 through three steps. First, we establish a Schatten-norm compression inequality for triangular block matrices. We then apply it to prove multiplicativity of the maximum output norm for diagonally sandwiched GADCs. Finally, phase covariance and the norm representation (21) convert this multiplicativity into additivity of Holevo Rényi information, following the framework of [WWY14].

3.1 Schatten-norm compression

We first establish the triangular norm-compression inequality used to control the factors in the output decomposition.

Theorem 3 (Schatten-norm compression).

For every 2⩽p⩽∞2\leqslant p\leqslant\infty and rectangular matrices U,V,WU,V,W of compatible sizes,

‖(U0VW)‖p\displaystyle\left\|\begin{pmatrix}U&0\\ V&W\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{p} ⩽‖(‖U‖p0‖V‖p‖W‖p)‖p.\displaystyle\leqslant\left\|\begin{pmatrix}\|U\|_{p}&0\\ \|V\|_{p}&\|W\|_{p}\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{p}. (23)

The constant one is sharp for every prescribed triple of nonnegative block norms and every compatible choice of positive block dimensions.

The main step is to establish the previously missing range 2<p<42<p<4. Polar decomposition reduces the norm comparison to an inequality for a trace-power difference. Joint convexity allows us to remove off-diagonal entries from two of its arguments; Jensen’s and Hölder’s inequalities then give the scalar comparison. The convexity argument extends the log-determinant method of [TZBW26, Appendix A] from entropy to trace powers. For p⩾4p\geqslant 4, the result follows from Audenaert’s two-row compression inequality [Aud08, Section 4.4], based on King’s positive-block inequality [Kin03].

Proof.

Consider first square blocks of the same size and 2<p<42<p<4. Set s=p/2s=p/2 and T=(U0VW)T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}U&0\\ V&W\end{smallmatrix}\right).

Step 1: Gram-matrix reduction. For positive semidefinite P,Q,RP,Q,R of a common dimension dd, define the positive semidefinite block matrix

Z⁡(P,Q,R)\displaystyle Z(P,Q,R) =(P+QQ​RR​QR).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}P+Q&\sqrt{Q}\sqrt{R}\\ \sqrt{R}\sqrt{Q}&R\end{pmatrix}. (24)

Choose polar decompositions V=UV​V†​VV=U_{V}\sqrt{V^{\dagger}V} and W=UW​W†​WW=U_{W}\sqrt{W^{\dagger}W}, extending the polar factors to unitaries. With J=UV†​UWJ=U_{V}^{\dagger}U_{W}, set P=U†​UP=U^{\dagger}U, Q=V†​VQ=V^{\dagger}V, and R=J​W†​W​J†R=JW^{\dagger}WJ^{\dagger}. Then

(I⊕J)​T†​T​(I⊕J†)\displaystyle(I\oplus J)T^{\dagger}T(I\oplus J^{\dagger}) =Z⁡(P,Q,R).\displaystyle=Z(P,Q,R). (25)

To compare the block matrix with its scalar compression, define the trace-power difference

Fs​(P,Q,R)\displaystyle F_{s}(P,Q,R) =Tr⁡Ps+Tr⁡Qs+Tr⁡Rs−Tr⁡Z​(P,Q,R)s.\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}P^{s}+\operatorname{Tr}Q^{s}+\operatorname{Tr}R^{s}-\operatorname{Tr}Z(P,Q,R)^{s}. (26)

We use the same notation for nonnegative scalar arguments; the scalar function is homogeneous of degree ss. The desired norm comparison reduces to

Fs​(P,Q,R)\displaystyle F_{s}(P,Q,R) ⩾Fs​(‖P‖s,‖Q‖s,‖R‖s).\displaystyle\geqslant F_{s}(\|P\|_{s},\|Q\|_{s},\|R\|_{s}). (27)

Indeed, replacing P,Q,RP,Q,R by their Schatten ss-norms preserves the first three terms of FsF_{s}. Thus, a lower bound on FsF_{s} gives an upper bound on the Schatten ss-norm of the Gram matrix. The identities ‖P‖s=‖U‖p2\|P\|_{s}=\|U\|_{p}^{2}, ‖Q‖s=‖V‖p2\|Q\|_{s}=\|V\|_{p}^{2}, and ‖R‖s=‖W‖p2\|R\|_{s}=\|W\|_{p}^{2} identify the required scalar comparison.

Step 2: Scalar compression. First suppose Q>0Q>0, and choose an eigenbasis with eigenvalues qiq_{i}. Let xi,zix_{i},z_{i} be the diagonal entries of P,RP,R in this basis, and set y=‖Q‖sy=\|Q\|_{s}. We have

Fs​(P,Q,R)\displaystyle F_{s}(P,Q,R) ⩾(a)​∑iFs​(xi,qi,zi)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{\geqslant}\sum_{i}F_{s}(x_{i},q_{i},z_{i})
=ys​∑iqisys​Fs​(xiqi,1,ziqi)\displaystyle=y^{s}\sum_{i}\frac{q_{i}^{s}}{y^{s}}F_{s}\!\left(\frac{x_{i}}{q_{i}},1,\frac{z_{i}}{q_{i}}\right)
⩾(b)​ys​Fs​(Tr⁡(Qs−1​P)ys,1,Tr⁡(Qs−1​R)ys)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\geqslant}y^{s}F_{s}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(Q^{s-1}P)}{y^{s}},1,\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(Q^{s-1}R)}{y^{s}}\right)
⩾(c)​ys​Fs​(‖P‖sy,1,‖R‖sy)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(c)}}{\geqslant}y^{s}F_{s}\!\left(\frac{\|P\|_{s}}{y},1,\frac{\|R\|_{s}}{y}\right)
=Fs​(‖P‖s,‖Q‖s,‖R‖s).\displaystyle=F_{s}(\|P\|_{s},\|Q\|_{s},\|R\|_{s}). (28)

For step (a), average simultaneous conjugations of P,Q,RP,Q,R by diagonal sign unitaries in the chosen eigenbasis of QQ. This fixes QQ and removes the off-diagonal entries of P,RP,R. The resulting Gram matrix is a direct sum of scalar 2×22\times 2 blocks. Unitary invariance and joint convexity in (P,R)(P,R), proved in Lemma 5 (Appendix A), give the inequality. The next equality uses homogeneity, and step (b) applies Jensen’s inequality with weights qis/ysq_{i}^{s}/y^{s}, which sum to one. For step (c), Hölder’s inequality gives Tr⁡(Qs−1​P)⩽ys−1​‖P‖s\operatorname{Tr}(Q^{s-1}P)\leqslant y^{s-1}\|P\|_{s} and similarly for RR. Scalar monotonicity from the same lemma gives the inequality in the stated direction. The final equality again uses homogeneity. Continuity, with QQ replaced by Q+ϵ​IQ+\epsilon I, extends (27) to Q⩾0Q\geqslant 0.

Write a=‖U‖pa=\|U\|_{p}, b=‖V‖pb=\|V\|_{p}, and c=‖W‖pc=\|W\|_{p}. Combining the two steps yields

‖T‖p2\displaystyle\|T\|_{p}^{2} =‖Z⁡(P,Q,R)‖s⩽‖(a2+b2b​cb​cc2)‖s=‖(a0bc)‖p2.\displaystyle=\|Z(P,Q,R)\|_{s}\leqslant\left\|\begin{pmatrix}a^{2}+b^{2}&bc\\ bc&c^{2}\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{s}=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\ b&c\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{p}^{2}. (29)

This proves the claimed inequality throughout 2<p<42<p<4. For 4⩽p<∞4\leqslant p<\infty, it is the triangular specialization of [Aud08, Section 4.4]; at p=2p=2, it is the Frobenius identity.

Zero padding embeds compatible rectangular blocks into square blocks of a common size, preserving the nonzero singular values of every block and of the full matrix. The limit p→∞p\to\infty gives the operator-norm endpoint. Finally, choose unit vectors |u1⟩,|u2⟩,|v1⟩,|v2⟩|u_{1}\rangle,|u_{2}\rangle,|v_{1}\rangle,|v_{2}\rangle in the corresponding row and column spaces, and set U=a⁡|u1⟩​⟨v1|U=a|u_{1}\rangle\!\langle v_{1}|, V=b⁡|u2⟩​⟨v1|V=b|u_{2}\rangle\!\langle v_{1}|, and W=c⁡|u2⟩​⟨v2|W=c|u_{2}\rangle\!\langle v_{2}|. The full matrix is then an isometric embedding of its scalar compression, proving sharpness for every a,b,c⩾0a,b,c\geqslant 0. ∎

3.2 Multiplicativity of maximum output norm

The compression inequality now yields multiplicativity of the maximum output norm for the GADC sandwiched by any nonnegative diagonal operator.

Theorem 4 (Sandwiched norm multiplicativity).

For every γ,N∈[0,1]\gamma,N\in[0,1], every nonnegative diagonal HH, every finite-dimensional completely positive map Φ\Phi, and every 1⩽p⩽∞1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty,

νp​((𝒜γ,N)H⊗Φ)\displaystyle\nu_{p}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}\otimes\Phi) =νp​((𝒜γ,N)H)​νp​(Φ).\displaystyle=\nu_{p}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H})\nu_{p}(\Phi). (30)

The input and output dimensions of Φ\Phi are arbitrary, and neither map is required to preserve trace.

The proof decomposes the joint output into a convex combination of two positive operators with triangular factors. The decomposition parameter is chosen from the block norms so that both factors have the same scalar Gram matrix after compression. Theorem 3 and the triangle inequality then reduce the joint output norm to a one-copy output norm times a scalar controlled by νp​(Φ)\nu_{p}(\Phi).

Proof.

First assume 1⩽p<∞1\leqslant p<\infty and 0<γ,N<10<\gamma,N<1. Convexity of the Schatten norm reduces the optimization to normalized pure inputs |ψ⟩=|0⟩⊗|u⟩+|1⟩⊗|v⟩|\psi\rangle=|0\rangle\otimes|u\rangle+|1\rangle\otimes|v\rangle, where ⟨u|u⟩+⟨v|v⟩=1\langle u|u\rangle+\langle v|v\rangle=1. Since Φ\Phi is completely positive, the intermediate output is positive semidefinite and admits the factorization

R\displaystyle R :=(id⊗Φ)​(|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|)=(Φ⁡(|u⟩​⟨u|)Φ⁡(|u⟩​⟨v|)Φ⁡(|v⟩​⟨u|)Φ⁡(|v⟩​⟨v|))=(XY)​(X†Y†).\displaystyle:=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi)(|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi|)=\begin{pmatrix}\Phi(|u\rangle\!\langle u|)&\Phi(|u\rangle\!\langle v|)\\ \Phi(|v\rangle\!\langle u|)&\Phi(|v\rangle\!\langle v|)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}X\\ Y\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X^{\dagger}&Y^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}. (31)

Set m=‖X‖2​p2+‖Y‖2​p2m=\|X\|_{2p}^{2}+\|Y\|_{2p}^{2}. If m=0m=0, the output vanishes and the desired bound is immediate. Otherwise, set q=‖Y‖2​p2/mq=\|Y\|_{2p}^{2}/m and first assume that both XX and YY are nonzero, so 0<q<10<q<1.

Step 1: Decompose the output into triangular factors. Write t=tγ,N​(q)t=t_{\gamma,N}(q) and D=Dγ,N​(q)D=D_{\gamma,N}(q). The interior assumptions ensure 0<t<10<t<1 and D>0D>0. Set λ0=γ⁡(1−N)​q​t/D\lambda_{0}=\gamma(1-N)qt/D and λ1=γ​N​(1−q)​(1−t)/D\lambda_{1}=\gamma N(1-q)(1-t)/D. The output admits the decomposition

(𝒜γ,N⊗id)(R)\displaystyle({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}\otimes\operatorname{id})(R) =∑j=01λj​Mj​Mj†,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{1}\lambda_{j}M_{j}M_{j}^{\dagger}, (32)

where

M0\displaystyle M_{0} =((1−γ)​qt​XDq​t​Ytq​Y0),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\dfrac{(1-\gamma)q}{t}}\,X&\sqrt{\dfrac{D}{qt}}\,Y\\[5.69046pt] \sqrt{\dfrac{t}{q}}\,Y&0\end{pmatrix}, M1\displaystyle M_{1} =(1−t1−q​X0(1−γ)​(1−q)1−t​YD(1−q)​(1−t)​X).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\dfrac{1-t}{1-q}}\,X&0\\[5.69046pt] \sqrt{\dfrac{(1-\gamma)(1-q)}{1-t}}\,Y&\sqrt{\dfrac{D}{(1-q)(1-t)}}\,X\end{pmatrix}. (33)

Direct block multiplication verifies (32). The identity D=γ⁡(1−N)​q​t+γ​N​(1−q)​(1−t)D=\gamma(1-N)qt+\gamma N(1-q)(1-t) shows that the positive weights sum to one. The factor M1M_{1} is triangular, and M0M_{0} becomes triangular after exchanging its block rows.

Write H=h0​|0⟩​⟨0|+h1|1⟩​⟨1|H=h_{0}|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+h_{1}|1\rangle\!\langle 1| with h0,h1⩾0h_{0},h_{1}\geqslant 0. For j=0,1j=0,1, let BjB_{j} be the scalar matrix obtained by replacing each block of (H⊗I)​Mj(H\otimes I)M_{j} by its Schatten 2​p2p-norm. The choice of qq ensures that both scalar Gram matrices coincide:

Bj​Bj†\displaystyle B_{j}B_{j}^{\dagger} =m(𝒜γ,N)H(|ψq+⟩⟨ψq+|),j=0,1.\displaystyle=m({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|),\qquad j=0,1. (34)

Indeed, substitute ‖X‖2​p=m⁡(1−q)\|X\|_{2p}=\sqrt{m(1-q)} and ‖Y‖2​p=m​q\|Y\|_{2p}=\sqrt{mq}, and use D=t⁡(1−t)−(1−γ)​q​(1−q)D=t(1-t)-(1-\gamma)q(1-q). The result is precisely the matrix in (11), multiplied by mm and sandwiched by HH.

Step 2: Norm compression via Theorem 3. We obtain the norm comparison

∥((𝒜γ,N)H⊗id)(R)∥p\displaystyle\|(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}\otimes\operatorname{id})(R)\|_{p} =(a)​‖∑j=01λj​(H⊗I)​Mj​Mj†​(H⊗I)‖p\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{=}\left\|\sum_{j=0}^{1}\lambda_{j}(H\otimes I)M_{j}M_{j}^{\dagger}(H\otimes I)\right\|_{p}
⩽(b)​∑j=01λj​‖(H⊗I)​Mj‖2​p2\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\leqslant}\sum_{j=0}^{1}\lambda_{j}\|(H\otimes I)M_{j}\|_{2p}^{2}
⩽(c)​∑j=01λj​‖Bj‖2​p2\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(c)}}{\leqslant}\sum_{j=0}^{1}\lambda_{j}\|B_{j}\|_{2p}^{2}
=∑j=01λj​‖Bj​Bj†‖p\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{1}\lambda_{j}\|B_{j}B_{j}^{\dagger}\|_{p}
=(d)​m​‖(𝒜γ,N)H​(|ψq+⟩​⟨ψq+|)‖p.\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(d)}}{=}m\|({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|)\|_{p}. (35)

Step (a) substitutes the output decomposition (32). Step (b) uses the triangle inequality and ‖A​A†‖p=‖A‖2​p2\|AA^{\dagger}\|_{p}=\|A\|_{2p}^{2}. Step (c) is Theorem 3 at order 2​p⩾22p\geqslant 2. For M0M_{0}, apply the same block-row permutation to (H⊗I)​M0(H\otimes I)M_{0} and B0B_{0}; Schatten norms are unchanged. The nonnegative diagonal operator HH preserves the zero blocks. The next equality again uses the relation between the two Schatten norms. Step (d) uses the common Gram matrix in (34) and the normalization λ0+λ1=1\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{1}=1.

It remains to bound the scalar factor mm and the one-copy output norm:

‖((𝒜γ,N)H⊗Φ)​(|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|)‖p\displaystyle\|(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}\otimes\Phi)(|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi|)\|_{p} ⩽(e)​m​‖(𝒜γ,N)H​(|ψq+⟩​⟨ψq+|)‖p\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(e)}}{\leqslant}m\|({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|)\|_{p}
=(f)​[‖Φ⁡(|u⟩​⟨u|)‖p+‖Φ⁡(|v⟩​⟨v|)‖p]⋅‖(𝒜γ,N)H​(|ψq+⟩​⟨ψq+|)‖p\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(f)}}{=}\bigl[\|\Phi(|u\rangle\!\langle u|)\|_{p}+\|\Phi(|v\rangle\!\langle v|)\|_{p}\bigr]\cdot\|({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|)\|_{p}
⩽(g)​(⟨u|u⟩+⟨v|v⟩)​νp​(Φ)​νp​((𝒜γ,N)H)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(g)}}{\leqslant}(\langle u|u\rangle+\langle v|v\rangle)\nu_{p}(\Phi)\nu_{p}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H})
=νp​(Φ)​νp​((𝒜γ,N)H).\displaystyle=\nu_{p}(\Phi)\nu_{p}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}). (36)

Step (e) is (35), using the definition of RR. Step (f) uses X​X†=Φ⁡(|u⟩​⟨u|)XX^{\dagger}=\Phi(|u\rangle\!\langle u|), Y​Y†=Φ⁡(|v⟩​⟨v|)YY^{\dagger}=\Phi(|v\rangle\!\langle v|), and ‖X‖2​p2=‖X​X†‖p\|X\|_{2p}^{2}=\|XX^{\dagger}\|_{p}. Step (g) follows from homogeneity and the definition of the maximum output norm, since |ψq+⟩|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle is normalized. The final equality uses the normalization of the input state.

If q=0q=0 or q=1q=1, exactly one of X,YX,Y is nonzero. Then RR is a computational-basis projection tensored with a positive matrix, and the comparison between the first and last expressions in (35) holds with equality. For fixed p<∞p<\infty, continuity in γ,N\gamma,N extends the bound to the boundary of [0,1]2[0,1]^{2}, without evaluating singular factorization formulas. Zero diagonal entries of HH are already permitted. Finally, taking p→∞p\to\infty gives the operator-norm endpoint.

Maximizing over inputs proves the upper bound. Product inputs give the reverse inequality because Schatten norms multiply on tensor products, completing the proof. ∎

For integer pp, sandwiched norm multiplicativity also follows from the entrywise-positive map theorem of King, Nathanson, and Ruskai [KNR05, Theorem 3]. The GADC sandwiched by any nonnegative diagonal operator satisfies that theorem’s matrix-unit positivity condition. Theorem 4 extends this conclusion to every real order p⩾1p\geqslant 1. In particular, the range 1<p<21<p<2 is essential for taking the order-one limit that determines the capacity.

3.3 Additivity of Holevo Rényi information

We now apply Theorem 4 to the information-radius representation. Phase covariance reduces the one-copy reference optimization to diagonal states, and product reference states give the tensor-power upper bound. Product input ensembles establish the reverse inequality.

Proof of Theorem 1.

Fix α>1\alpha>1.

Step 1: Diagonal reference states. Let Z=diag⁡(1,−1)Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1) and σ¯=(σ+Z​σ​Z)/2\overline{\sigma}=(\sigma+Z\sigma Z)/2. For every output state ω\omega and strictly positive σ\sigma,

D~α(ω∥σ¯)\displaystyle\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}(\omega\|\overline{\sigma}) ⩽1α−1​log⁡2(α−1)D~α(ω∥σ)+2(α−1)D~α(ZωZ∥σ)2\displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\frac{2^{(\alpha-1)\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}(\omega\|\sigma)}+2^{(\alpha-1)\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}(Z\omega Z\|\sigma)}}{2}
⩽max{D~α(ω∥σ),D~α(ZωZ∥σ)}.\displaystyle\leqslant\max\{\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}(\omega\|\sigma),\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}(Z\omega Z\|\sigma)\}. (37)

The first inequality follows from data processing under discarding a uniformly distributed binary flag. Before the flag is discarded, the first state has ω\omega in both blocks, while the reference has σ\sigma and Z​σ​ZZ\sigma Z. Evaluating their sandwiched Rényi divergence and using unitary invariance gives the logarithmic average in the first line. The second inequality bounds the average of the two exponential terms by their maximum.

The covariance relation (9) at θ=π\theta=\pi makes the output set invariant under conjugation by ZZ. Taking the supremum over outputs in (37) therefore shows that diagonalizing the reference cannot increase its radius. Together with (22) and (20), this gives

χ~α​(𝒜γ,N)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}) =inf0<s<1supρD~α(𝒜γ,N(ρ)∥σs)\displaystyle=\inf_{0<s<1}\sup_{\rho}\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(\rho)\|\sigma_{s})
=inf0<s<1αα−1​log⁡να​((𝒜γ,N)Hα,s),\displaystyle=\inf_{0<s<1}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}\log\nu_{\alpha}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H_{\alpha,s}}), (38)

where σs=diag⁡(1−s,s)\sigma_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(1-s,s) and Hα,s=σs(1−α)/(2​α)H_{\alpha,s}=\sigma_{s}^{(1-\alpha)/(2\alpha)}.

Step 2: Rényi Holevo additivity. Using σs⊗n\sigma_{s}^{\otimes n} as a trial reference, we obtain

χ~α​(𝒜γ,N⊗n)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n}) ⩽inf0<s<1supρnD~α(𝒜γ,N⊗n(ρn)∥σs⊗n)\displaystyle\leqslant\inf_{0<s<1}\sup_{\rho_{n}}\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n}(\rho_{n})\|\sigma_{s}^{\otimes n})
=inf0<s<1αα−1​log⁡να​((𝒜γ,N)Hα,s⊗n)\displaystyle=\inf_{0<s<1}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}\log\nu_{\alpha}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H_{\alpha,s}}^{\otimes n})
=n​inf0<s<1αα−1​log⁡να​((𝒜γ,N)Hα,s)\displaystyle=n\inf_{0<s<1}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}\log\nu_{\alpha}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H_{\alpha,s}})
=n​χ~α​(𝒜γ,N).\displaystyle=n\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}). (39)

The inequality restricts the reference optimization, without restricting the input ρn\rho_{n}. The first equality is the norm representation (20). The second applies Theorem 4 repeatedly, with a sandwiched completely positive map as the other factor. The last equality is (38).

For the reverse direction, every finite input ensemble ℰ\mathcal{E} satisfies

χ~α​(𝒜γ,N⊗n)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n}) ⩾I~α​(ℰ⊗n,𝒜γ,N⊗n)=n​I~α​(ℰ,𝒜γ,N).\displaystyle\geqslant\widetilde{I}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{E}^{\otimes n};{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n})=n\widetilde{I}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{E};{\cal A}_{\gamma,N}). (40)

The inequality uses the ensemble representation (18). The equality follows from [MO17, Lemma IV.8], which establishes additivity of the ensemble information for product ensembles even when the reference optimization allows correlated states. Taking the supremum over ℰ\mathcal{E} gives the lower bound and completes the proof of (4).

Substituting (4) into (3) gives the exponent formula (5). ∎

Proof of Corollary 2.

For each fixed positive integer nn, take α→1+\alpha\to 1^{+} in (4). The convergence of sandwiched Rényi Holevo information to Holevo information [MO17, Lemma IV.6] gives

χ⁡(𝒜γ,N⊗n)\displaystyle\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n}) =n​χ​(𝒜γ,N).\displaystyle=n\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}). (41)

Substituting this identity into the Holevo–Schumacher–Westmoreland formula (1) proves (6). ∎

Appendix A Convexity of the trace-power difference

The function FsF_{s} in (26) is the trace-power analogue of the entropy difference studied in [TZBW26, Appendix A]. A positive integral representation in terms of the same log-determinant functional yields the convexity needed in Section 3.1.

Lemma 5 (Convexity and scalar monotonicity).

For 1<s<21<s<2 and fixed Q⩾0Q\geqslant 0, Fs​(P,Q,R)F_{s}(P,Q,R) is jointly convex over positive semidefinite P,RP,R. For fixed y⩾0y\geqslant 0, the scalar function Fs​(x,y,z)F_{s}(x,y,z) is nonincreasing in each of x,z⩾0x,z\geqslant 0.

Proof.

For u>0u>0, define

Gu\displaystyle G_{u} =(P+u​I00R+u​I),Ju=(0u​Q−u​Q0).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}P+uI&0\\ 0&R+uI\end{pmatrix},\qquad J_{u}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sqrt{uQ}\\ -\sqrt{uQ}&0\end{pmatrix}. (42)

With κs=−ssin(πs)/π>0\kappa_{s}=-s\sin(\pi s)/\pi>0, we have

Fs​(P,Q,R)\displaystyle F_{s}(P,Q,R) =κs∫0∞us−1[lndet(Gu+Ju)detGu−lndet(I+Q/u)]du.\displaystyle=\kappa_{s}\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{s-1}\left[\ln\frac{\det(G_{u}+J_{u})}{\det G_{u}}-\ln\det(I+Q/u)\right]\,\mathrm{d}u. (43)

To see this, apply the scalar identity

xs\displaystyle x^{s} =κs​∫0∞us−1​[x/u−ln⁡(1+x/u)]​𝑑u,x⩾0,\displaystyle=\kappa_{s}\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{s-1}\bigl[x/u-\ln(1+x/u)\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}u,\qquad x\geqslant 0, (44)

to the eigenvalues of P⊕Q⊕RP\oplus Q\oplus R and Z⁡(P,Q,R)⊕0dZ(P,Q,R)\oplus 0_{d}. Their equal traces cancel the linear terms, and their equal dimensions match the determinant normalizations. The Schur-complement identity det(Z⁡(P,Q,R)+u​I)=det(Gu+Ju)\det(Z(P,Q,R)+uI)=\det(G_{u}+J_{u}) from [TZBW26, Eqs. (A.7)–(A.9)] then gives (43). Since Z⁡(P,Q,R)+u​I>0Z(P,Q,R)+uI>0, this identity also ensures det(Gu+Ju)>0\det(G_{u}+J_{u})>0, so its logarithm is well defined. The logarithmic bracket is O⁡(1+|ln⁡u|)O(1+|\ln u|) as u→0+u\to 0^{+} and O⁡(u−2)O(u^{-2}) as u→∞u\to\infty. The integral therefore converges for 1<s<21<s<2, even when P,Q,RP,Q,R are singular.

For fixed QQ, the matrix JuJ_{u} is fixed and skew-Hermitian, while GuG_{u} depends affinely on (P,R)(P,R). By [TZBW26, Lemma A.1], the first logarithmic term is therefore jointly convex in (P,R)(P,R); the second is constant. Integration against the positive weight κs​us−1\kappa_{s}u^{s-1} proves joint convexity. For scalar arguments (x,y,z)(x,y,z), the determinant ratio is

det(Gu+Ju)detGu\displaystyle\frac{\det(G_{u}+J_{u})}{\det G_{u}} =1+u​y(x+u)​(z+u).\displaystyle=1+\frac{uy}{(x+u)(z+u)}. (45)

This ratio is nonincreasing in xx and zz, while the remaining logarithmic term is independent of them. The same integral representation therefore proves scalar monotonicity. ∎

Appendix B Scalar evaluation of the Rényi Holevo information

We express the sandwiched Rényi Holevo information as an optimization over the reference parameter ss and the input parameter qq. The objective is explicit, and the order infsmaxq\inf_{s}\max_{q} is retained.

Lemma 6 (Scalar Rényi radius).

Fix γ,N∈[0,1]\gamma,N\in[0,1] and α>1\alpha>1, and let σs=diag⁡(1−s,s)\sigma_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(1-s,s) for 0<s<10<s<1. For the states |ψq+⟩|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle defined in (10),

χ~α​(𝒜γ,N)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}) =inf0<s<1max0⩽q⩽1D~α(𝒜γ,N(|ψq+⟩⟨ψq+|)∥σs)\displaystyle=\inf_{0<s<1}\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|)\|\sigma_{s})
=1α−1​log⁡[inf0<s<1max0⩽q⩽1⁡{λ+​(α,s,q)α+λ−​(α,s,q)α}].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\!\left[\inf_{0<s<1}\max_{0\leqslant q\leqslant 1}\{\lambda_{+}(\alpha,s,q)^{\alpha}+\lambda_{-}(\alpha,s,q)^{\alpha}\}\right]. (46)

The eigenvalues of the sandwiched output are given by

Tα​(s,q)\displaystyle T_{\alpha}(s,q) =[1−tγ,N​(q)]​(1−s)1−αα+tγ,N​(q)​s1−αα,\displaystyle=[1-t_{\gamma,N}(q)](1-s)^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}}+t_{\gamma,N}(q)s^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}},
λ±​(α,s,q)\displaystyle\lambda_{\pm}(\alpha,s,q) =Tα​(s,q)±Tα​(s,q)2−4​Dγ,N​(q)​[s⁡(1−s)]1−αα2.\displaystyle=\frac{T_{\alpha}(s,q)\pm\sqrt{T_{\alpha}(s,q)^{2}-4D_{\gamma,N}(q)[s(1-s)]^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}}}}{2}. (47)

Here Tα​(s,q)T_{\alpha}(s,q) is the trace of the sandwiched output. The dependence of TαT_{\alpha} and λ±\lambda_{\pm} on the fixed channel parameters γ,N\gamma,N is suppressed.

Proof.

Equation (38) restricts the reference to σs\sigma_{s} with 0<s<10<s<1, including the channel endpoints. For fixed ss, maximizing the divergence is equivalent to maximizing the Schatten α\alpha-norm of the sandwiched channel output. This norm is convex in the input, so a pure state suffices. Up to a global phase, every pure qubit state has the form Uθ​|ψq+⟩U_{\theta}|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle. Phase covariance and [Uθ,σs]=0[U_{\theta},\sigma_{s}]=0 make the objective independent of θ\theta, leaving only the optimization over qq. Writing H=σs(1−α)/(2​α)H=\sigma_{s}^{(1-\alpha)/(2\alpha)}, the remaining evaluation is

D~α(𝒜γ,N(|ψq+⟩⟨ψq+|)∥σs)\displaystyle\widetilde{D}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|)\|\sigma_{s}) =1α−1​log⁡Tr⁡[((𝒜γ,N)H​(|ψq+⟩​⟨ψq+|))α]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\left(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}(|\psi_{q}^{+}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{q}^{+}|)\right)^{\alpha}\right]
=1α−1​log⁡[λ+​(α,s,q)α+λ−​(α,s,q)α].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\bigl[\lambda_{+}(\alpha,s,q)^{\alpha}+\lambda_{-}(\alpha,s,q)^{\alpha}\bigr]. (48)

The sandwiched output has trace Tα​(s,q)T_{\alpha}(s,q) and determinant Dγ,N​(q)​[s⁡(1−s)](1−α)/αD_{\gamma,N}(q)[s(1-s)]^{(1-\alpha)/\alpha}. Its eigenvalues are therefore those in (47). Taking the reference infimum and input maximum proves (46). ∎
